text: <calm>The generator has one job.</calm> Start from an input prime p. Output the next prime q. The record is only two keys: p and q. That small output is the point. Diagnostics can explain what happened, and audit can verify the answer, but generation itself emits the minimal pair.
The rule begins in the finite interval to the right of p. That interval is not a place to ask a primality oracle for help. It is the local arithmetic region where prime-gap structure is measured.
Inside the interval, only wheel-open boundary positions can become endpoint hypotheses. The mod thirty wheel removes positions that are already closed by two, three, or five.

Every integer in the chamber carries exact divisor-count state. A prime has divisor count two. A composite has more than two. PGS does not need a probabilistic primality test inside generation; it uses this local divisor-count structure.

The divisor normalization identity gives the fixed-point picture. For an integer n, Z of n equals n raised to one minus d of n over two. When d of n is two, Z is one. Prime states land on the fixed-point locus. Composite states fall below it.

GWR selects the leftmost integer with minimum divisor count inside the chamber. That selected integer is a landmark. It orients the local structure. It is not automatically the endpoint, and the rule q equals w plus one is false.

The endpoint rule is the production step. Build wheel-open candidate hypotheses. Reject candidates with composite divisor-count state. Preserve semiprime-shadow landmarks as unresolved landmarks. Lock the GWR-selected integer only after a resolved candidate exists. After the lock, apply the lower-divisor threat ceiling. Identify the first resolved survivor. Reset the search interval at that survivor. <emphasis>The survivor is q.</emphasis>

There is no fallback branch. If the PGS selector does not resolve inside the supplied bound, generation raises PGSUnresolvedError. It does not call trial division, Miller-Rabin, nextprime, isprime, ECPP, PARI, or a sieve.

The output stream remains physically minimal: one resolved input prime, one two-key record. Source labels, counters, selected-integer data, and proof objects live in sidecar diagnostics, not in the generated line.

The current measured surface is audit clean. From eleven through one million, seventy eight thousand four hundred ninety four input primes produced seventy eight thousand four hundred ninety four PGS outputs, with zero unresolved cases and zero audit failures. The high-scale decade-window probe is also audit clean: two hundred fifty six consecutive input primes per decade, from ten to the eighth through ten to the eighteenth, for two thousand eight hundred sixteen outputs and zero audit failures.

That is an empirical generator result, not a theorem proof. The proof pressure is now narrower. Fallback removal is complete for the current production generator. The active question is why the PGS-only next-prime selection rule keeps resolving across scale.

The discipline is ratio-first and invariant-first. Measure the state, measure the rate of local change, and normalize both against the same fixed limit. In this repository, DNI, GWR, and chamber reset are not decoration. They are the arithmetic machinery that turns local structure into the next endpoint. PGS math is the claim that the next prime can be selected from local prime-gap structure, with no backup prime search inside generation. On the declared surfaces, the rule outputs the actual next prime and audit confirms every record.
